message.reasoning_content:
I'm checking how the join, group_by and rolling paths run through the lazy and in-memory engine, which looks right. Next I'm sketching out the first pipeline: the keys are sorted ascending with nulls first, and the positions are UInt32 sorted ascending with nulls last.

I'm working through the gather path: a sorted array taken by sorted indices keeps its ascending flag, but that only holds when the indices contain no nulls. The null placement on each side matters, and I'm checking whether nulls end up as a contiguous prefix.

I'm now checking the mixed case: when the target has nulls at the start and the indices have nulls at the end, the output gets nulls at both ends, so the sorted flag would be wrong there. I'm wondering whether that matches the intended behavior or an injected change, and the "only one side has missing entries" case seems consistent with it.

I'm now looking at the upstream version of the same gather-flag helper and its take path, which looks identical. That makes me suspect the null-handling edge I flagged might already be present upstream rather than being an injected change, so I'm still unsure which it is.

I'm weighing whether the flag-propagation helper is the culprit, since the same take path calls it from several gather routines plus the chunked take.

I'm weighing where the null-placement fix belongs: the flag helper only sees sort direction, not where nulls sit, so I'm thinking about adding that check at the take call site. The chunked take paths seem safe since their chunk ids carry no nulls, so the problem looks limited to the direct gather routines.

I'm checking the null case in the gather.rs callers that take an index array, since the sorted flag can be wrong there. With target nulls at the start and index nulls at the end, the max and min still come out as None, so the result looks correct for this case, and I'm now checking how Series max_reduce reaches ChunkAgg::max.

I'm checking the group-by fast path on the sorted keys: with two nulls at the start, the code skips past them and partitions the remaining values into groups.

I'm tracing the group-by fast path on the sorted keys: with two nulls at the front, the null group takes rows 0 and 1, and row 1's real key gets folded into that null group. I still need to confirm that the single-key group_by in the in-memory engine actually goes through this column-level group_tuples routine.

I'm tracing how a filter on a constant column behaves inside a group-by aggregation, and checking whether the filtered result stays a scalar or turns into index-based groups.

I'm checking the sorted flag on the scalar path: the filtered constant column gets a new sorted-ascending index, and the validity mask doesn't clear that flag. The aggregation helper seems to be missing a step that marks the result as unsorted.

I'm settling on where the fix should go: the flag helper never sees where nulls sit, so the decision needs to be made where the scalar column is masked. The constant's Ascending flag comes from creating it with the index constructor and survives the validity update, so the masked result still claims to be sorted.

I'm checking whether the sorted flag is wrong for the masked constant: the null-placement problem sits in the scalar path, so the fix should go where the validity gets applied.

I'm checking how the sorted flag on the masked constant interacts with the max and group-by paths, and the result looks like it could give wrong answers there too.

I'm checking how the Column::Series path handles these flags, since the scalar case seems to keep the sorted flag on masked values. Next I'm looking at whether Series::agg_first on index groups resets that same flag.

I'm now checking the rolling path: with a one-unit window and a sorted `v`, the windows come out as slices, and the first-value aggregation takes the indices for each window, which include some empty ones.

I'm checking the rolling path next: when the windows are empty, the first-value aggregation still marks the output as sorted ascending, even though nulls end up scattered between the values.

Next I'm checking the remaining aggregation paths: min and max route through the same flag-carrying helpers, with max reaching agg_last since the series has no nulls, so the flag isn't touched there. Last and the rest seem to behave correctly. I still need to confirm whether evaluate_on_groups_impl in the aggregation code is how the rolling executor reaches these functions.

I'm checking whether the rolling-first path in polars-expr has its own fast path that bypasses this. Downstream, the max comes back as None because the last non-null position lands on a null, and the group-by splits into two groups keyed by 2 and the underlying value at the null slot.

I'm checking how the take call handles a null index: the closure dereferences the index with `?`, so a null index should short-circuit to None rather than read a value. That would put the null-index rows into the null group instead of the row-1 key, which changes the group count I worked out above.

I'm working out the rolling case with a period of 3 and the default offset, so each window covers the rows up to the current one, and then picking the first value of each slice based on the parity of the last time index.

I'm checking the slice path next: the expression-based offsets are built with monotonic set to false, but agg_first only tests whether the groups are sorted by first index, which always holds for slices. That means the sorted flag gets carried over even though the first indices here aren't monotonic, so this is the source of the bad result.

I'm checking the slice-with-offset case next: slice(1,1) takes the second row of each window, and the null-free result [None, 2, 2, 3, 4] still comes out sorted ascending with the nulls first, so the flag stays valid here.

I'm comparing the two failures: in the empty-group case the flag check doesn't account for empty groups, and in the overlapping-slice case `is_sorted_by_first_idx` always returns true for slices, so both come down to that one decision in `agg_first`. I'm now checking whether a single helper is responsible for both.

I'm checking whether `GroupsType::is_sorted_by_first_idx` is the only place that decides the sorted flag for slice groups, since it returns true for every slice. Then I'm comparing how `agg_first_non_null` and `agg_last_non_null` make the same kind of decision, to see whether the empty-group and overlapping-slice failures share one root cause.

I'm reading the GroupsProxy sorted-flag logic and suspect the Slice arm returns true when it should return false, since slice groups can overlap and their first indices need not be monotonic. That would explain both failures, so I'll check whether `is_sorted_by_first_idx` in position.rs really returns true unconditionally for slices.

I'm now checking whether the same flag shortcut applies to ordinary sorted columns under filtering: when a group comes back empty, the first value is null, so a sorted input could come out with nulls scattered between its values while still claiming to be ascending.

I'm recalling how upstream `agg_first` handles its sorted flag, which seems to treat slice groups differently from index groups. Then I'm comparing that against the `is_sorted_by_first_idx` result for slices to see whether the same check explains both failures.

Still checking whether the Slice arm of the sorted-flag helper should return false, since overlapping or non-monotonic slice groups can't safely carry the sorted flag through first.

The sorted flag on Slice groups is decided by `is_sorted_by_first_idx`, which reports true for every slice, so `agg_first` keeps the input's ascending flag even when empty groups or overlapping windows break the order. Both the empty-group and overlapping-slice failures seem to come from that one check, though empty Idx groups would have the same problem if they ever showed up.

I'm wondering whether the empty-window case would also slip past a monotonic check, since the start positions for empty rolling windows may still be nondecreasing. If so, the fix can't just be the monotonic test and has to deal with the empty groups too.

I'm weighing whether the empty-window failure and the overlapping-slice failure are really two separate causes or one shared decision: the Slice arm of the sorted-flag check, which claims every slice group is sorted. If that check is the culprit for both, there's a single root cause, and I'm trying to confirm it before I count the distinct issues.

I'm going to check the other routines that apply this same sorted-flag decision, starting with the merge-based join path, which I suspect repeats the logic inline. I'll also look at whether a missing NaN check in that path could explain a separate failure.

I'm checking the join path for NaN: polars sorts NaN as the largest value, so the left keys count as ascending, but the sorted merge join compares with IEEE equality, so NaN never matches anything. The hash join uses total equality, which is why the two paths would disagree on NaN keys.

I'm checking the hash-join fallback: when the right side has at least as many rows as the left, or the keys contain nulls or the left isn't sorted, the hash join handles NaN keys with total equality, so those cases match. The sorted merge path is different: it compares with IEEE equality, so a NaN left key never matches, and the left join then gives it a null row id.

Writing sorted-join code...

Checking the upstream sorted merge join, I want to see whether float keys are compared by bit pattern or by IEEE value, since that determines whether NaN ever matches.

Next I'm checking whether float keys get canonicalized to bit representations before they reach the join, since that would decide whether NaN keys ever match.
